title: Drone Strikes Tanker Carrying 11 Indian Seafarers Off Oman; Two Missing
excerpt: The Nicaragua-flagged MT Petro Dolphin was hit at Sohar Anchorage on Sunday; nine of its 11 Indian crew were rescued as Oman's Coast Guard searches for two missing sailors.
body:
• The Nicaragua-flagged tanker MT Petro Dolphin, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was struck by a drone at Sohar Anchorage off Oman on October 11. Nine crew were rescued; two Indian nationals remain missing.
  • Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal confirmed the attack on X, saying Oman's Coast Guard is conducting active search-and-rescue operations with Indian authorities coordinating support.
  • A second tanker, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT Valthera, was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz the same day. All 11 Indian seafarers aboard are safe.
  • India's Ministry of External Affairs condemned the attacks as "deeply concerning" and urged de-escalation through dialogue. Brent crude rose 2.28% to $102.28 on the news.

What happened at Sohar Anchorage

The MT Petro Dolphin came under drone fire on Sunday while anchored off Sohar in northern Oman. All 11 crew members aboard were Indian nationals. Nine were pulled to safety; two remain unaccounted for as Oman's coast guard continues active rescue operations.

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal announced the incident on social media platform X: "While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing. Search-and-rescue operations are actively underway by the local Coast Guard." The Embassy of India in Muscat said it is in close and continuous contact with the Omani authorities, and is also coordinating with the management companies of both vessels.

A second ship hit the same day

On the same day, the MT Valthera, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, starting a fire on board. All 11 Indian seafarers on the Valthera were reported safe. Together, the two attacks affected 22 Indian crew members — 20 safe, two missing.

Neither the minister's statement nor the embassy has assigned responsibility for either attack, and officials have not established whether the two vessels were targeted by the same party or as part of a coordinated operation. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued a warning after the Sohar strike.

A pattern, not an isolated incident

The attacks fit an escalating pattern in the Gulf's commercial shipping lanes. Just five days earlier, on October 6, the Panama-flagged tanker MT On Peace was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Of its 19 crew, 17 were Indian nationals, and 12 crew members — including 11 Indians — were injured.

India's Ministry of External Affairs condemned both the latest attacks and the earlier one, calling the recurring strikes on commercial shipping "deeply concerning" and warning they risk "further aggravating an already volatile situation." The ministry reiterated its call for "immediate de-escalation and a resolution to the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran through dialogue and diplomacy," adding that the safety of Indian seafarers remains a government priority.

"The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers and civilian infrastructure in the region must end."

— Ministry of External Affairs, India

Markets feel the strain

The attacks sent immediate ripples through energy markets. Brent crude futures rose 2.28% to $102.28 a barrel as shipping risk in the Strait of Hormuz — through which roughly 20% of global oil and fuel flows — intensified. According to Baltic Exchange data, daily earnings for Very Large Crude Carriers on the Middle East Gulf-to-China route have surged above $1.2 million as insurers and operators price in the risk.

Diaspora angle

Indian nationals make up a large share of the world's merchant crews, and Gulf routes are the arteries of India's energy and trade. For the thousands of seafaring families in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Maharashtra watching these reports, the Embassy of India in Muscat is the point of contact — its public statement on X confirms it is tracking both vessels and coordinating rescue and consular assistance.

What's next

The immediate focus is the search for the two missing seafarers off Sohar. Beyond that, shippers and insurers will be watching whether the attacks continue at this cadence — analysts cited by shipping press note that while producers are absorbing higher insurance costs for now, further escalation could materially reduce Persian Gulf shipments. India's government, meanwhile, is pressing for de-escalation, but with responsibility for the strikes unassigned, the diplomatic path remains murky.
